Although radiocarbon dating measures the residual carbon-14 content of organic material, it remains reliable for organic samples up to about 200,000 years old. Because radiocarbon measurements must be calibrated against a tree-ring-based curve such as IntCal20, calibrated results are reported as probability ranges rather than fixed points. A calibrated radiocarbon age is expressed as a single exact calendar year; this cannot be squared with the practice of reporting such results as probability ranges, since the two characterisations of what a date is cannot both be true. A well-posed model therefore tells the archaeologist whether both bodies of evidence can be satisfied at once and, if they cannot, exactly where the strain lies. Because such modelling weighs the priors drawn from the section against the individual determinations, it yields an outlier analysis that identifies determinations inconsistent with the stated stratigraphic order. Rodent burrowing and other bioturbation can transport small charcoal fragments across layer boundaries. By contrast, charcoal from the heartwood of long-lived trees yields an \"old wood\" age offset older than the event being dated. A flagged determination accordingly sends the analyst back to the history of the sample itself rather than to the section drawing. At one such site, the burrows traced through the relevant horizon had carried fragments downward, and it was this displacement that made the dated charcoal intrusive in the layer from which it was recovered. The scale of the discrepancy measured against short-lived seeds from the same context shows, for its part, that the dated charcoal came from wood that was already centuries old when it burned. At least one of the two conditions must obtain here — a fragment out of place, or long-seasoned timber in the hearth — and perhaps both together. Because the outlier analysis had isolated and down-weighted the determinations that conflicted with the superposition sequence, the Bayesian model placed the start of occupation in the late fourth millennium BC; in other words, it placed the beginning of settlement at the site between 3300 and 3000 BC. A finding of that kind settles the matter: a demonstrable taphonomic account of why the discordant determinations run too old, coupled with a model in which the surviving determinations and the excavated order of deposits agree, leaves the competing reconstruction without evidential support."
